angle: The CEO asked a market question. I built an agent that answered it from our CRM data in 10 minutes
post_first_line: 10 minutes. One agent. One CEO question answered.
linkedin_post:
10 minutes. One agent. One CEO question answered.

The answer changed where the team is hiring.

Jeff Kirchick got a question from the CEO. The company sells an ICHRA, a healthcare benefit that works better in some states than others because some states are friendlier to it.

The question was where the company is underinvesting in its market.

Jeff built an agent that analyzed the company's HubSpot data. It compared the number of quotes being run in each state against how friendly that state is to the product.

The gap between the two showed where the market is underinvested.

The company is hiring right now, so Jeff now has data to guide where a new person should sit.

The whole thing took all of 10 minutes.

That's the shift. A market question used to mean a long analysis project. Now it can be a quick build on top of data you already have in your CRM.

What's the last question your CRM could have answered?

angle: I could automate all my coaching. Here's why I walked it back.
linkedin_post:
30, 40, 50 rules. 7 customer stories.

Neema Zarrabian could have automated all of the coaching. Instead, the approach changed.

For a month, Neema built a Notion for every rep, listing the questions they couldn't answer, and sent it straight to them in Slack.

It worked on paper. But nothing beats talking to a rep about a deal, watching the call together, and taking notes on how they say things.

That's where the real coaching happens. Asking live: why did you go this way? Why not that way?

Neema still does some of the async version. But the focus now is talking to reps live, putting notes in the one-on-one docs, and asking directly: do you feel good about this?

The takeaway: automation can scale the rules and the stories. It can't replace the human part of coaching, which is where reps get held accountable and become coachable.

Where have you walked back automation?

Slide 2: 30 to 50 rules and 7 customer stories were ready to go.
Slide 3: For a month, Neema built Notions of questions each rep couldn't answer.
Slide 4: Nothing beats watching a call with a rep and taking notes.
Slide 5: Asking why they went one direction, live, surfaces the real thinking.
Slide 6: Now Neema coaches live and captures it in one-on-one docs.
Slide 7: Reps are held accountable and coachable through human conversation.
Slide 8: Automate the rules. Keep the coaching human.

lesson.title: Automate the Playbook, Not the Coaching
takeaways: Rules and customer stories can be documented, but they don't replace live conversation about a real deal.
Watching a call with a rep shows how they say things and why they chose a direction.
Reps become accountable and coachable through human interaction, so keep one-on-ones personal.
lesson.exercise: Pick one rep's recent call this week. Watch it together, ask why they went one direction and not another, and log the notes in your one-on-one doc.

angle: How a seller with no engineering background built a working Salesforce-to-Slack-to-Gmail bot from one Claude Code session
post_first_line: Matt Stinson built a Salesforce bot in one session.
linkedin_post:
Matt Stinson built a Salesforce bot in one session.

Three months ago, Matt didn't know what Apex class code was.

Then one Claude Code session produced a working bot across Salesforce, Slack, and Gmail.

Matt described exactly what the bot should do, then planned out the infrastructure with Claude Code. The setup looked like this:

A custom Apex class in Salesforce posts a webhook that acts as the trigger.

Railway hosts the interface that monitors that trigger.

It pushes to a Slack bot, where the end user interacts with it.

Gmail handles the final mile, and the result flows back into Salesforce.

This is coming from someone who barely knew how to run customized reports in Salesforce. Matt used to spend 45 minutes on a fairly simple report.

Now it's pretty easy, and Matt's take is that the only real limit is having a good idea.

What would you build if the technical barrier disappeared?
carousel: Slide 1: 3 months ago, Matt didn't know what Apex class code was.
Slide 2: One Claude Code session produced a working Salesforce-Slack-Gmail bot.
Slide 3: Step one: describe exactly what you want the bot to do.
Slide 4: Step two: plan the infrastructure with Claude Code.
Slide 5: A custom Apex class in Salesforce posts a webhook trigger.
Slide 6: Railway hosts the interface monitoring that trigger and pushes to Slack.
Slide 7: Gmail handles the final mile, then the result flows back to Salesforce.
Slide 8: The only limit now is having a good idea.

lesson.title: Build a cross-tool bot without an engineering background
takeaways: Start by describing exactly what you want the bot to do, then plan the infrastructure with Claude Code before building.
The architecture is simple: a Salesforce Apex webhook triggers, Railway hosts and monitors, Slack is the user interface, and Gmail handles the final mile back into Salesforce.
You don't need to know the technology upfront. The limiting factor is having a good idea.
lesson.exercise: Pick one repetitive task that spans two or three of your tools. Write a plain-English description of the trigger, the user interaction, and the end result, then use it to start a planning session in Claude Code.

angle: Ask AI what you're not thinking about. Start with one micro problem.
post_first_line: Matt Stinson started with one spreadsheet and a question.
linkedin_post:
Matt Stinson started with one spreadsheet.

Matt hadn't connected Claude or any AI tool to Salesforce yet. So Matt downloaded some rep data, conversion data, and funnel data, then opened a chat with Claude Code.

Matt listed the things already on the radar. Then came the ask: find something that isn't on this list.

The question wasn't what Matt expected to ask an AI, and the answer surprised Matt too.

They went back and forth. Somewhere in that process, a pattern showed up: this could be bundled into a skill or a flow.

The idea became simple. Run the same process every week before the next one-on-one.

Matt's takeaway: start with a specific micro problem, then scale from there. That's a solid way to decide where to build.

No big architecture plan. Just one small problem, one conversation, and a repeatable workflow that fell out of it.

What's one micro problem you could start with?

Start on a specific micro problem, then scale it, rather than planning a big build upfront.
